title: Electron Microscopy of the g-C3N4/Ni Heterojunction for Photoreduction of Heavy Metals and Hydrogen Production
content: Advanced Oxidation Processes (AOP) and particularly photocatalytic processes using semiconductor materials have shown high efficiency for the removal of recalcitrant compounds from water. Several semiconductor materials have been studied as photocatalysts, being TiO2 [1] the most widely reported. However, TiO2 has limitations, such as its wide band gap (3.2 eV), which limits its photo activity to the UV region of the solar spectrum. Thus, research in the development of new semiconductor materials with activity in the visible region of the spectrum (lower band gap) and photocatalytic stability are currently under study. In this context, g-C3N4 has emerged as an interesting alternative, it has a low band gap values (≥3.0 eV), but with a high recombination rate of the photo-generated charge carriers [2-4]. To improve the stability of g-C3N4, the formation of hybrid materials (inorganic materials such as metals and/or metal oxides supported on organic materials) has been reported as an interesting alternative [5]. On the other hand, the photocatalytic treatment of pollutants in water has been recently investigated [6, 7]. Multifunctional materials containing hybrid materials are the most attractive systems [8, 9]. This type of materials can be used for photodegradation of heavy metals or the production of H2 [10,11] from polluted water. For this type of hybrid materials to work correctly, it is desirable that the processes be controllable and consequently simple (oxidation/reduction of species) and that the materials are versatile since in some cases they must perform more than one function in a process. In this investigation, such a combination of controllable processes and versatile materials is applied to obtain energy with the highest possible efficiency. In addition such processes must be friendly to the environment.
